Short close front vowel [i], stressed in the Greek form.
Velar nasal [ŋ] before the final stop.
Voiceless velar stop [k] plus voiceless sibilant [s], the standard ending.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SFINGKS' — aspirate the 'p' as you release it, stress the first syllable, and end with a sharp 'ks'.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Σφίγξ (Sphínx), 'the strangling one' — the common noun from σφίγγω, 'to squeeze, throttle' (LSJ)

kin.label: Egyptian
kin.form: The androsphinx of Egypt — lion's body, king's head — a guardian image the Greeks borrowed; the Great Sphinx at Giza predates the Theban monster by over a thousand years

kin.label: Modern
kin.form: The word 'sphinx' has become a synonym for any enigma or riddling presence

pronunciation.note: Sphínx is Tier 2: the restoration preserves exactly one feature ASCII loses — the acute on the stressed ί. English 'Sphinx' flattens the pitched accent; it does not, as older notes claimed, alter the consonant cluster, which the Latin transcription already writes 'nx'. The Egyptian sphinx, though visually related, is a separate cultural entity with its own name and history.

domains.title: Riddling Monster
domains.subtitle: Guardian, Strangler, and Threshold Terror
domains.lead: The Sphinx is the winged lion-woman who crouched outside Thebes and strangled those who could not answer her riddle. She is not merely a monster but a guardian of thresholds: the creature who bars the road until the traveller proves worthy of understanding — and who destroys those who cannot name what they are.

cards.name: Guardian of Thebes
cards.desc: Sent by Hera, she perched on Mount Phicium and posed her riddle to every traveller on the road (Apollodorus 3.5.8).

cards.name: The Riddle
cards.desc: 'What walks on four feet in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening?' — a compressed life of man.

cards.name: Strangler
cards.desc: Her name means 'the strangling one'; all who failed the riddle she seized and devoured.

cards.name: Defeated by Oedipus
cards.desc: Oedipus answered 'man'; in fury or shame she threw herself from the rock (Apollodorus 3.5.8; Hyginus, Fab. 67).

symbols.name: Lion's body
symbols.meaning: Royal power and the dangerous strength of the threshold guardian — the Egyptian form the Greeks borrowed

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: The aerial, predatory nature of the creature; she strikes from above like a bird of prey

symbols.name: Woman's head
symbols.meaning: Intelligence and speech — the source of the deadly riddle; the human face is what makes her question articulate

symbols.name: Cliff at the crossroads
symbols.meaning: The liminal place between cities, between ignorance and knowledge, between life and death

mythology.lead: The Greek Sphinx is a daughter of monstrous parents, sent by Hera to punish Thebes. Her story is inseparable from the tragedy of Oedipus — the man who answered her question and thereby walked straight into the fate he had fled. Every telling of the riddle is a small treatise on what it means to be human.

myths.title: Child of Chimaira — or of Echidna?
myths.text: Hesiod gives the Sphinx an unexpected pedigree: in the Theogony (325–327) she is born to the Chimaira by Orthrus, the two-headed hound — a pairing that also produces the Nemean Lion — which makes her Typhon's granddaughter, twice removed from the storm-giant's challenge to Zeus. Apollodorus, Library 3.5.8, streamlines the line and calls her simply 'daughter of Typhon and Echidna', kin to Cerberus and the Hydra. The sources disagree, and the disagreement is itself instructive: both genealogies place her inside the same brood of hybrid terrors, children whose mixed bodies embody the world's refusal to keep its categories clean. What the Sphinx inherited is a compound nature — speech joined to claws, a question delivered by a predator. Her lineage tells us what her riddle will confirm: the monster at the threshold is never only a monster, and neither is the answerer only a man.

myths.title: Sent Against the Cadmeans
myths.text: While Laius was king of Thebes, Hera sent the Sphinx against the city as a plague, Apollodorus reports (Library 3.5.8): a creature with the face of a woman, the breast and feet and tail of a lion, and the wings of a bird. She took up station on Mount Phicium above the city and waylaid travellers with a riddle the Muses had taught her. Those who failed to solve it she snatched up and devoured, until the roads fell silent and Thebes starved behind its walls. Creon, ruling for the young Laodamas, proclaimed that whoever freed the city of the monster should have the kingdom — and the hand of the widowed Jocasta. The Sphinx was therefore never a random horror: she was a siege engine of divine anger, a blockade of knowledge laid against a city already burdened with an old, unconfessed crime. Her questions stopped the mouths of Thebes as surely as famine; only a stranger willing to answer for all mankind could lift the blockade.

myths.title: Oedipus Names the Creature
myths.text: Oedipus, the Corinthian exile with the pierced ankles, came to the crossroads beneath Mount Phicium and heard the Sphinx's question: what creature walks on four feet at morning, two feet at noon, and three feet at evening? 'Man,' he answered — crawling in infancy, upright in maturity, leaning on a staff in age (Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus 130–151, 390–398; Apollodorus 3.5.8). In a later, harsher version of the question the feet are 'crippled', and the answer must carry Oedipus's own lameness inside it. Defeated by the one answer she could not survive, the Sphinx — cursing him even in defeat, Sophocles says — threw herself from the rock and died (Apollodorus 3.5.8; Hyginus, Fabulae 67; Pausanias 9.26.2–4 discusses the monument the Thebans later raised to her). The myth's economy is perfect: a single word ends a siege, wins a throne, and delivers the answerer to the incest and patricide he believed he had outrun. To solve the riddle of man is to inherit man's whole fate.

myths.title: The Older Guardian of Giza
myths.text: The Greek sphinx did not invent its own body. For more than two thousand years before the Theban monster was conceived, Egypt carved the androsphinx — lion's body, king's head — to guard temples, tombs, and processional ways; the Great Sphinx at Giza, cut from the living rock beside Khafre's pyramid around 2500 BCE, is the supreme survivor of that tradition, and Herodotus (2.175) saw sphinxes still standing in the sanctuaries of Egypt. But the Egyptian sphinx asks no riddles and strangles no one: it is royal power at rest, vigilance made monumental, the king as sun-guardian at the horizon. What the Greeks did was fuse that hieratic form to a characteristically Greek terror — the lethal question, the exam at the threshold — and the fusion proved unforgettable. The borrowed body shows how freely the Greeks looted older cultures for monsters; the invented voice shows what they added. Egypt made the sphinx a wall; Greece made it an interrogator.

lore.syncretism: The Greek Sphinx merged with the much older Egyptian sphinx guardian, and the composite figure travelled through Roman, Byzantine, and medieval art — Virgil places a sphinx among the eternal torments at the underworld's gate (Aeneid 6.289). In medieval Europe she became an emblem of sin, especially deceit and luxuria; by the Enlightenment she stood for enigma itself. Egyptology returned her to Giza, where the Great Sphinx remains the world's most famous sculpture. Modern psychology borrowed her question as the emblem of the Oedipus complex, and her name has become the common noun for any inscrutable person. At every stage the fusion holds: Egypt's silent guardian wearing Greece's dangerous voice.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Sphinx is one of the most durable images in world art. The Great Sphinx of Giza anchors every account of ancient Egypt, while the Greek riddling sphinx dominates literature from Sophocles through Freud to the present. The word itself has become a verb for any mysterious or inscrutable presence, and the 'riddle of the Sphinx' names every problem whose answer is the questioner. In popular culture she appears as gatekeeper, puzzle-master, and symbol of ancient wisdom — preserving the ancient idea that knowledge is the price of passage, and that the creature at the threshold is always, in the end, a mirror.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The Sphinx does not ask for strength or beauty; she asks for understanding. Her riddle is not a trick but a compressed account of human life: four legs, two legs, three legs. To answer is to accept mortality — to name the creature that limps, ages, and leans. Oedipus answers and so enters Thebes, and enters at the same moment the fate he thought he had escaped.

The Sphinx teaches that thresholds are guarded by insight, not force. Every important transition demands that we say what we are. Those who cannot answer remain outside, devoured by their own incomprehension; the monster is never the danger — the inability to understand oneself is. It is no accident that the Greeks made their most articulate monster a woman with a lion's claws: the question that saves you is also the question that condemns you, and it comes dressed in the body you fear.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek is Σφίγξ, from σφίγγω, 'to squeeze, strangle'. The word was borrowed into Latin as Sphinx and into English with a short i. PUNICODEX restores the acute of the Greek form as Sphínx, preserving the stress the English spelling flattens. The Egyptian sphinx, though visually related, is a separate cultural entity with its own name (sspꜥnḫ, 'living image') and its own two-and-a-half millennia of history.
